newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraq warns Kuwait on invasion anniversary.
newsitem.headline: Iraq warns Kuwait on invasion anniversary.

text.p: Iraq on Saturday marked the seventh anniversary of its invasion of Kuwait by accusing rulers of the oil-rich state of "wickedness" and plotting against Baghdad.
State-run newspapers carried front-page editorials and articles hitting out at Washington and Kuwaiti rulers, blaming the August 2, 1990 invasion on them.

"The rulers of Kuwait, instead of learning the lesson...are today persisting in their wickedness and plotting (against Iraq)," the official al-Iraq newspaper said in an aritcle written by former information undersecretary Noori al-Marsomi.

"There is still enough time for the Kuwaiti rulers to review their calculations and stand (toward Iraq) as Iraq and its people are more determined than ever to confront and foil any plotting," it said.
Iraqi troops were driven out of Kuwait in February 1991 after a six-week war by a U.S.-led multinational force based mainly in Saudi Arabia.
Al-Iraq 1991 Gulf War was still on as "the unjust embargo is still in place" -- referring to United Nations trade sanctions imposed on Baghdad after the invasion.
Babel, Iraq's most influential newspaper, said August 2 marked "legitimate national retaliation against plots of Washington relying on its ally, the Kuwaiti rulers".

"The United States is still using the Kuwaiti card as a means to harm our people and homeland despite the fact that it has implemented the (U.N.) Security Council resolutions," Babel, owned by President Saddam Hussein's eldest son Uday, added.
The Iraqi invasion followed weeks of wrangling over oil production quotas between Iraq and Kuwait, both members of the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC).
"The rulers of Kuwait flooded world markets with cheap energy...inflicting on Iraq heavy losses estimated at billions of dollars," the official newspaper al-Qadissiya said in an editorial.
Baghdad in 1994 recognised Kuwait as an independent state within the borders demarcated by a U.N. commission.

The U.N. sanctions include a ban on Iraq's oil exports. But since December the United Nations has allowed Baghdad to sell $2 billion worth of oil over six months on a renewable basis to buy urgent needs for Iraqis.
Kuwait, backed by Washington, wants Iraq to account for 600 missing Kuwaitis and meet other demands before the trade restrictions can be lifted.
